summary: The bill bars social media platforms from letting anyone under 13 open or keep an account, restricts personalized recommendation systems for anyone under 17, and requires schools that receive federal broadband subsidies to block student access to social media on school devices and networks.

scores.thoughts: The bill establishes no new federal spending programs, appropriations, or mandates that would expand outlays. It conditions access to existing E-rate broadband subsidies on compliance with social media blocking requirements but does not alter overall funding levels or create new expenditures. Therefore, it has no bearing on government spending.
The bill contains no tax provisions, rate changes, credits, or revenue measures. It is silent on taxation.
The bill addresses social media access and school internet policies; it has no connection to healthcare delivery, coverage, or markets.
No provisions relate to firearms, regulations, or Second Amendment issues.
The bill does not address immigration, visas, borders, or related protections.
No content pertains to reproductive rights or abortion access.
The legislation has no defense, military, or national security spending components.
No environmental, regulatory, or climate-related provisions appear in the bill.
The bill does not modify welfare programs, eligibility, or benefits.

Title II updates the Children’s Internet Protection Act to require schools receiving E-rate subsidies to block social media platforms on school networks and devices. This adds a federal compliance condition on an existing education-technology subsidy program, representing a modest increase in federal involvement in school internet policy without altering funding levels or promoting school choice.
No references to controlled substances, decriminalization, or enforcement.
The bill creates civil enforcement mechanisms via the FTC and state attorneys general but does not alter criminal sentencing, policing, or rehabilitation policies.
No trade, tariff, or globalization provisions are present.
The bill neither authorizes new deficit spending nor directs resources toward debt reduction.
The legislation is silent on LGBTQ+ legal protections or rights.
No foreign aid or international assistance measures are included.
The bill does not address voting access, election administration, or voter ID requirements.

Title I directly regulates social media platforms by prohibiting accounts for children under 13, restricting personalized recommendation systems for users under 17, and imposing data-handling rules. These requirements constitute new federal oversight and data-protection mandates on technology companies, making the bill primarily about increasing regulation of tech platforms.
No labor, union, or employment provisions are present.
The bill contains no language concerning religious exemptions or civil-rights enforcement.
